meta.dates: Each person has "presence" {from, to, grade, basis}. Where a person's home or day differs by date, "days" lists {from_date, to_date, label, day}. meta.alignment: Where the Kinzie family slept in the fort from 7 April 1812 is not recorded; this reading puts John Kinzie in the officers' barracks (reconstructed). The women's and children's readings should agree one building for the family.

presence.basis: Came to live at Chicago in 1804 (Wau-Bun; Kinzie's Chicago account book opens May 1804, Quaife ch. VI); left with his family for St Joseph on 18 August 1812 (Wau-Bun, Andreas p. 74). Day precision of the first date is ours.

absent.basis: Fled after killing Lalime (Porthier: to Milwaukee; Hubbard: hidden in the bush for days) and came back "as soon as his wound was healed" (Andreas p. 74); back in the fort by 7 August (Wau-Bun). The return date is not recorded.

present.basis: Living inside the fort with his family when Winnemeg came on 7 August (Wau-Bun) and still there at the evacuation (Andreas p. 74); marched on the 15th.

age_1812.basis: Born at Quebec in 1763 by family tradition (Quaife, Wau-Bun); 48 or 49 on 14 August, the birthday not being known.

looks.hair: brown going grey, worn short or in a short queue
looks.basis: NO LIKENESS EXISTS: Kirkland (1893) "No portrait of John Kinzie has ever been found" and Currey (1912) "There are no pictures of John Kinzie, the pioneer". Colouring is drawn from his heritage only: a Scottish father (Kirkland app. D, Currey), born at Quebec; the height is the period mean for American men (68.1 in, as T-3491 used). days.label: gone: at Milwaukee, or hidden in the woods, until the officers cleared him

trader_1812.builds_on: docs/RESEARCH/people-1812-3461/dress.json role "Prosperous trader / merchant about 1810 (John Kinzie) and his wife (Eleanor Kinzie)"
trader_1812.pieces: Base (3461): dark wool tailcoat cut away at the waist, high collar; waistcoat; white shirt and white neckcloth; knee breeches with stockings and shoes, or pantaloons with top boots; tall round hat. Variants. (a) Kinzie at work in August: an old plain coat or a round jacket over the waistcoat, linen trousers, shoes; a leather apron at the silversmith's bench; the full coat and hat for the councils of 12 and 14 August and for the march. (b) The clerk (Chandonnai): round jacket, coloured calico shirt, a sash or scarf at the waist, trousers, moccasins or shoes; a man between the trader's and the engagé's dress. (c) The official (Irwin, Lalime): the town version, coat, waistcoat, neckcloth, shoes; Lalime with a pistol and dirk in his belt on 17 June. All carry a hat outdoors.
trader_1812.colours: Coat dark green, dark blue or brown-black; waistcoat yellow, buff or white; breeches black or buff; trousers natural linen; neckcloth white. The clerk's and the trader's working shirt may be coloured calico (blue, pink, printed), by the 1830 analogy below.
trader_1812.basis: The base is direct for the type (3461's Met objects and paintings, all proposed source ids in dress.json new_sources). Nothing describes Kinzie's, Irwin's or Lalime's own clothes, and Kinzie has no portrait; the variants are reconstruction. The coloured calico shirt of the fur-trade gentleman is Wau-Bun's observation of 1830 (Fox River, John H. Kinzie and Judge Doty), an analogy eighteen years late.

engage_1812.builds_on: docs/RESEARCH/people-1812-3461/dress.json role "French Canadian / Métis engagés and voyageurs, and a Métis or French woman of the country"
used_by: French or Métis members of the militia (see each card)
engage_1812.pieces: In August at Chicago: a suit of smoked deerskin (hunting shirt or jacket and trousers or leggings) belted, with moccasins and a pipe, as the Kinzie household dressed Sergeant Griffith on 15 August 1812 "like a French engagé"; or (the other common summer dress) a calico shirt, a bright-coloured sash or scarf at the waist, linen trousers, moccasins, a straw hat (Lambert's summer exchange; Wau-Bun's "mitiff" of 1830) or a red tuque. The beaded worsted arrow sash (McCord M8486) and a capot for cool mornings, from 3461. Ribbons and red or yellow gartering at the knee are part of the outfit (Wau-Bun on the voyageur's advance at Mackinac). Ouilmette, a householder of long standing, wears the same with a waistcoat. Mirandeau at the forge: shirt sleeves and a leather apron.
engage_1812.colours: Deerskin smoked tan to brown; shirts printed or striped calico, blue, red or white; sash red-dominant with blue, green and yellow chevrons (colours reconstructed, 3461); tuque red; straw hat natural with a dark band; gartering red or yellow; trousers natural linen or blue.
engage_1812.basis: The deerskin suit is direct for Chicago, August 1812 (Wau-Bun, after the Kinzie family's telling); the calico-shirt-and-sash dress is direct for 1830 Wisconsin and for 1806-08 Lower Canada, and is inferred for Chicago 1812. Who wore which is ours.

settler_1812.builds_on: docs/RESEARCH/people-1812-3461/dress.json role "Soldiers in fatigue dress at work (August)" for the old soldier's pieces, and the trader role's "frontier working version"; there is no settler role in dress.json.
used_by: American members of the militia (see each card)
settler_1812.pieces: A frontier farmer or labourer in August: coarse linen or tow shirt, open at the neck or with a kerchief; a waistcoat or none; loose linen or tow trousers (or old knee breeches on the older men); shoes or moccasins; a round or wide-brimmed felt or straw hat. Burns, an old soldier discharged in 1811, may keep an old fatigue frock or round jacket. As militia from April 1812: the same clothes with a musket, bayonet, cartridge box and belts from the garrison store, no uniform. A hunting shirt over all is a fair alternative for the Americans.
settler_1812.colours: Shirts unbleached or white, checked blue; trousers natural, tan or blue; waistcoats brown, red or striped; hats black or straw; belts whitened buff or black.
settler_1812.basis: No source describes the clothes of any Chicago settler of 1812. The arms are direct (Quaife: armed from the garrison store); the clothes are a reconstruction from rural American dress of 1811-15 in 3461's proposed Met sources (Pixler family, Krimmel's country inn).
